item.title: Iran to receive Russian Su-35 jets after war ends, IRGC says
item.description:
Iran to receive Russian Su-35 jets after war ends, IRGC says

Iran has bought Russian Su-35 fighter jets and expects to receive them after the war ends, spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Mohammad Akraminia, has said, adding the country's air force will emerge stronger after the war.

In an interview with Iranian news site Tabnak, Akraminia said the aircraft were originally supposed to arrive before the war began, adding that the necessary preparations and training have been completed.

item.title: MotoGP faces Qatar security concerns ahead of Grand Prix
item.description:
MotoGP faces Qatar security concerns ahead of Grand Prix

MotoGP is set to go ahead with the Qatar Grand Prix even as a group of riders demand more assurances for travelling to the region, with organisers arguing that a "zero-risk environment" is unrealistic.

The race at the Lusail International Circuit, originally scheduled for April, was postponed to 6 November to 8 due to the US-Israeli war against Iran.

"MotoGP has provided teams and riders with every assurance available from the State of Qatar, the circuit ... and our own ongoing risk assessment processes," a MotoGP spokesperson said.

"We fully respect the concerns raised and highlight that safety remains the priority for everyone involved."

However, the MotoGP spokesperson said the expectation of a zero-risk environment was not realistic anywhere in the world by any government or organiser.

"Over the past months, we have maintained continuous dialogue with teams and riders, sharing the latest information available, providing direct access to documents and answering questions openly and transparently," the spokesperson said.

Carlos Ezpeleta, deputy CEO of MotoGP, visited Qatar on Thursday, where the circuit's president, Abdulrahman Al-Mannai, said they were ready to welcome the riders, teams and fans for the 20th round of the season.

However, Spain's embassy in Qatar has issued a notice urging its citizens not to travel to the Gulf nation unless absolutely necessary.

Spaniards make up the largest share of riders on the grid, including world champion Marc Marquez.

Report by Reuters

item.title: Lebanese foreign minister urges Gulf states to help restore country's sovereignty
item.description:
Lebanese foreign minister urges Gulf states to help restore country's sovereignty

Lebanon's Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji has called for a complete Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territories, an end to ongoing attacks and the full implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, while urging Gulf states to support efforts to restore Lebanon's sovereignty.

Speaking at the 22nd Manama Dialogue, organised by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), Rajji said restoring state authority was essential to Lebanon's stability and its relations with Arab countries, Lebanon's National News Agency reported.

He said Lebanon, under President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, had embarked on a path to reassert state control, pointing to government decisions aimed at placing all weapons under state authority and banning Hezbollah's military and security activities.

"Lebanon will no longer allow its territory to be used against the security of its Arab brothers or as a bargaining chip in negotiations conducted beyond its borders," Rajji said during a session on the Eastern Mediterranean.

The minister also reaffirmed Lebanon's solidarity with Bahrain and other Gulf states in "confronting Iranian attacks and those carried out by armed groups linked to Tehran", rejecting any violation of their sovereignty, security and territorial integrity.

He warned against allowing countries to "pursue regional ambitions through armed groups operating outside state authority", saying Lebanon had "experienced the devastating consequences of such organisations being used as instruments of foreign influence".

The Lebanese people, he said, had paid a heavy price for "wars they had never chosen to fight".

Rajji also raised concerns over maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, arguing that Gulf security could no longer be separated from developments in the Red Sea, which was closely linked to the security of the Eastern Mediterranean.

He called for a comprehensive Arab strategic partnership to address regional challenges, built around strong and sovereign states whose legitimate institutions retain exclusive authority over decisions of war and peace.

item.title: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
item.description:
IISS study questions overreliance on American support and ‘overdependence on expensive, high-end systems’

Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).

item.title: JD Vance letter may offer last chance to avert fresh conflict between US and Iran
item.description:
US vice-president writes to top Iranian security official in sign Washington has not abandoned diplomacy

Hopes of averting a major new conflagration between Iran and the US soon after Tuesday’s midterm elections could rest on Iran’s response to a personal letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, offering to restart diplomacy.

The letter, written after predominantly Qatari mediation, was sent to the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei on Sunday. It requires Tehran to agree to make commitments on its nuclear programme at the start of a process that would lead to the opening of the strait of Hormuz within seven days in return for US sanctions relief.
